clue.text: Like a candle's base

definitions.meaning: first meaning: having a wick, as every candle does

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks about the bottom of a candle; 'base' is really the adjective meaning low or immoral.
explanation.definitionFit: A candle is fitted with a wick, and the same word means evil or sinful, which is what base means of conduct.

clue.text: Navy boats? Adores, with a burning love

indicators.note: to burn something is to consume it, so the one letter eats up and takes the place of the other

parts.note: to adore someone is to worship them
taken as written
love is zero in tennis scoring, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether sailors burning with love adore their navy's ships.
explanation.walkthrough: WORSHIPS has its O replaced by A, giving WARSHIPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Warships are the fighting vessels of a navy; the question mark admits 'boats' is a loose word for big ships.

clue.text: American held up while involved in vice, refuses to talk

indicators.note: being involved in something places one inside it

parts.note: a vice is a clamp for holding work

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something up makes it read from bottom to top

parts.note: US is short for American

explanation.surface: A US citizen caught up in criminal vice says nothing to the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vice' looks like crime, but it is the workshop tool that grips things.
explanation.definitionFit: To clam up is an idiom for falling silent and refusing to say anything more.

clue.text: "Good …", say, for highest characters

parts.note: surface reading: an unfinished phrase, perhaps a greeting like good morning
setter's reading: the word completing the phrase praising someone of the finest character

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis asks for the word that follows 'Good' in the phrase used of a thoroughly decent person, a good egg.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a good egg is an old British idiom for a kind, trustworthy, honourable person.

clue.text: Answer could reference own solving, taking initial characters

definitions.text: Answer could reference own solving, taking initial characters

indicators.note: initial characters are the first letters of each word, so we keep only the opening letter of every word here

parts.words: Answer could reference own solving, taking initial characters
parts.note: the opening letters of all eight words

explanation.surface: A description of a puzzle whose solution hints at how to solve it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: its own word initials spell ACROSTIC, and the answer even starts like 'across', its direction.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrostic is a text in which the first letters of successive lines or words spell out a hidden message.

clue.text: Cryptic verse in music recording

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a CD is a compact disc of music
an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: Obscure poetry turns up on a music album.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cryptic' sits at the front like an adjective for the verse, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic message is written in code, so its meaning is hidden from the casual reader.

clue.text: Working off energy on allotment, breaking up stone

indicators.note: breaking something up splits it open so that other material can sit in the gap

parts.note: an opal is a gemstone
E is the symbol for energy in physics
a ration is an allotted share

explanation.surface: Someone burns off energy on their allotment by smashing up stones; an allotment is a rented garden plot in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Allotment' looks like a garden plot but means a share; 'off' merely joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine that is operational is up and running, in working order and ready for use.

clue.text: Tiddler bit on rod

parts.note: a tad is a little bit
a pole is a rod

explanation.surface: A small fish has bitten the bait on an angler's rod.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the first piece above the second. 'Bit' reads as the past tense of bite but is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiddler is any very small creature, especially a young fish, and a tadpole is a tiny young frog.

clue.text: Kind of panicking, losing head

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, which is lost here

parts.note: scaring someone sets them panicking

explanation.surface: A sort of panic in which someone loses their head.
explanation.walkthrough: SCARING loses its first letter. 'Kind of' looks like a single phrase, but 'Kind' is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A kind person is caring, showing warmth, concern and compassion for other people.

clue.text: Horse laid up with fresh reported infection

indicators.note: in a down clue, something put up runs from bottom to top

parts.note: a nag is an old horse

indicators.note: what is reported is spoken, so this piece is taken by its sound

parts.note: green means fresh or new

explanation.surface: A horse confined to its stall has picked up a new infection.
explanation.walkthrough: NAG upwards is GAN; the second half says 'green' but is spelt GRENE.
explanation.definitionFit: Gangrene is tissue death, often caused by bacterial infection of a wound.

clue.text: A rare drug manufactured for ultimate fighters?

indicators.note: something manufactured is made from raw materials, here letters assembled anew

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An unusual drug is made for elite combat troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimate' means last, not best: these are the soldiers at the very back.
explanation.definitionFit: The rearguard is the body of troops protecting the rear of an army, so the last fighters in line.

clue.text: Duck! Unlike ultimately headless horseman

indicators.note: without a head means the first letter is removed
ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
a rider without the first letter

explanation.surface: A warning to duck, unlike the headless horseman of legend who has nothing to duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck!' looks like a command to stoop, but it is the bird. The Headless Horseman is the ghost from Sleepy Hollow.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large sea duck whose soft breast feathers give eiderdown.

clue.text: Social media feature — dice game for children

parts.note: to dice food is to chop it up, making a hash
tag is a playground chasing game

explanation.surface: A social media trend turns out to be a dice game for kids.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dice' looks like the cubes rolled in a game; it is the cooking verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A hashtag is a word preceded by the # symbol, used on social platforms to label and group posts.

clue.text: Shower in river to get cool in preparation for work

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: the Tees is a river in north-east England
a shower of rain
hip means fashionable, cool

explanation.surface: Someone takes a cold river shower to freshen up before work.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tees is a crossword favourite among English rivers; 'cool' means fashionable, not cold.
explanation.definitionFit: A traineeship is a period of training that prepares someone for a job.

clue.text: Duck! Taking cover from mythical monster horseman

indicators.note: the item that takes cover hides inside the other, sheltered by it

parts.note: a dragon is a fire-breathing creature of myth
a duck is a score of zero in cricket, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A shout to duck as someone takes cover from a mythical beast.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a duck is a batter's score of nothing, hence the zero-shaped letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragoon was a mounted soldier, originally a cavalryman armed with a carbine.

clue.text: State secretary turning up with a freshly minted coin

parts.note: PA is a personal assistant

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
freshly minted means brand new
a guinea was an old British gold coin worth 21 shillings

explanation.surface: A secretary arrives carrying a newly struck coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freshly minted' sits naturally beside 'coin' in the surface but just means new.
explanation.definitionFit: Papua New Guinea is a sovereign country in the south-west Pacific, and a state is a nation.

clue.text: Travel on fixed date

parts.note: to travel is to go
steady means firmly fixed

explanation.surface: Arranging to travel on a set day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Date' looks like a day on the calendar; it is the verb for courting.
explanation.definitionFit: To go steady is to date one person regularly as a committed couple.

clue.text: Troll's reformed inside when offering sweets

indicators.note: the one word goes inside the other

parts.note: as means when, as in 'as I left'

indicators.note: reformed means formed again, rebuilt into a new shape

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A reformed troll hands out sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: Liquorice allsorts are a British mix of layered liquorice sweets.
explanation.definitionFit: Allsorts are assorted liquorice confectionery, so they are sweets.

clue.text: One is absorbed by Rocky sequel — instant classic

indicators.note: something absorbed is taken in and held within
rocky means unsteady, so the letters wobble into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A Rocky film sequel hailed as an instant classic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky' looks like the boxing film series; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something quintessential is the perfect, typical example of its kind, which is what a classic is.

clue.text: Court briefly, engrossed by wedding fervour

indicators.note: briefly means in a shortened form, so the word is abbreviated
someone engrossed by something is wrapped up in it

parts.note: a wedding is a union
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A brief courtship, swept up in wedding fever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' looks like the verb for wooing, which suits the wedding, but it is the abbreviated noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Unction is a manner of deep, earnest religious feeling, so a form of fervour.

clue.text: Fall is brought up after hip is weak

parts.note: hip and in both mean fashionable

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing something up makes it read from bottom to top

parts.note: a dip is a fall, plus is as written

explanation.surface: A fall is brought on by a weak hip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hip' looks like the joint but means trendy; the first 'is' belongs to the wordplay, the second is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Insipid means feeble, lacking flavour, vigour or interest, so it is weak.

clue.text: Fine-looking articulated old carriage

indicators.note: articulated means spoken clearly, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a fine-looking person is handsome

explanation.surface: An elegant articulated vehicle from the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articulated' suggests a jointed vehicle, like a lorry, but it signals speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A hansom was a two-wheeled horse-drawn cab of the Victorian era, with the driver seated behind.

clue.text: Gunners return from jovial, half-hearted target practice

indicators.note: with half its heart gone, one of the two middle letters drops out
to return is to go back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, the gunners of the British Army
cheery, with one of its central pair of letters removed

explanation.surface: Gunners come back from cheerful but lacklustre shooting practice.
explanation.walkthrough: RA backwards gives AR; CHEERY loses one E from its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Archery is the sport of shooting arrows at a target, so it is literally target practice.

clue.text: "Every second counts in my work", tell rustic type

indicators.note: only each second letter counts, so the others are skipped

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A worker insists every second matters on the job, says a country fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every second counts' sounds like a saying about time; it means take the even letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A yokel is an unsophisticated person from the countryside, a rustic.

clue.text: Nitless new recruits

indicators.note: something made new is remade, so the letters take a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Army recruits arrive freshly cleared of head lice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recruits' looks like a plural noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlist someone is to sign them up for service, which is to recruit them.

clue.text: Sound airy and stylish

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the hiss of something moving fast through air

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as describing a voice or a frock; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A whooshing noise through air is a swish, and in British slang swish also means smart or upmarket.

clue.text: Pied Piper type, in make-up, wearing oversized tie

indicators.note: whatever is worn surrounds the wearer

parts.note: a kipper tie is a very wide 1960s-70s necktie
DNA is one's genetic make-up

explanation.surface: A costumed Pied Piper in stage make-up and a huge tie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make-up' looks like cosmetics but means genetic constitution.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pied Piper of Hamelin led away the town's children, so he is the archetypal child abductor.

clue.text: Modern day love is a carry-on

parts.note: AD, anno domini, labels dates in the present era
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: These days, love is just a lot of fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: Ado is fuss or bother, and a carry-on is a British word for a fuss or commotion.

clue.text: Exclusivity in my pool — no swimming

indicators.note: letters swimming about move freely and land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An owner insists on private use of their pool: no swimming allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: A monopoly is exclusive possession or control of something, especially sole supply of a product.

clue.text: Criminal turf around apartments

parts.note: a con is a convict

indicators.note: turned around means facing the opposite way

parts.note: a sod is a piece of turf

explanation.surface: A gang's territory surrounds some flats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turf' suggests gang territory, but it is grass; SOD reversed is DOS.
explanation.definitionFit: Condos, short for condominiums, are individually owned apartments in a shared block, a North American term.
